questions.prompt: Walk through shipping the worker-timezone feature that Atlas deliberately deferred: which seams the TimeProvider design already gives you, where a calendar 'today' is derived now and which of those places would change, what the ambient-time fitness function would and would not catch in the new zone-conversion code, and which new tests pin the behaviour.

keyPoints.text: [w3] The domain side is already shaped for it: the probation question compares whatever calendar date it is handed with the end of the window, and a code note says the edge currently feeds it a UTC date as an approximation, so supporting zones changes which date callers pass, not the rule.

[w3] The UTC conversion is not in one place: each of the three worker endpoints turns the injected instant into a date on its own, and the same expression recurs across leave, terms, compliance, payroll and reporting use cases, so the first step funnels them into one calendar service ('today for this worker', 'today for this org') and the zone decision then lives in a single spot.

[w3] Only the statutory paths move: the code already separates the org-facing views, which keep UTC as a stated choice, from statutory dates such as probation and notice, so the feature switches the statutory callers to the worker's calendar and leaves terms and reports where they are, explicitly.

[w2] The data is missing: a worker carries a country code, and one country can span several zones, so the feature adds an IANA zone id per worker (defaulted from the country only where the country has a single zone) and converts the injected instant with an explicit zone lookup.

[w3] By its own header, the ban scans source files of Atlas.Domain only and looks only for the static Now and UtcNow clock properties; conversion code placed in Application or Api is never scanned, and even inside the domain a call to TimeZoneInfo.Local, the server's own zone and the very mechanism of the Manila incident, matches nothing, so the pattern and its scope both need widening with the feature.

[w2] Today's probation tests pass explicit dates at the Manila boundary (hired 2026-01-31, still inside on 07-30, over on 07-31); the new tests freeze the clock at 17:00 UTC on 2026-07-30, which is already 31 July in Manila, and assert the statutory answer follows the worker's zone while the org-facing view still follows UTC, plus a worker in a daylight-saving zone across a change.

[w1] The deferral notes come out with the fix: the ADR promised the shortcut would be flagged in code and in an exercise, so each path the feature corrects also loses its note, or the code starts describing a residual that no longer exists.
keyPoints.quote: so it cannot masquerade as finished

questions.prompt: Explain what a 90-second clock skew between two API pods does to Atlas: which date-dependent behaviours can diverge (effective-dating tie-breaks, lockout windows, audit ordering), which are protected by the read-once-per-operation and unique-index designs, which are not, and how a test reproduces cross-node skew with two differently-pinned clocks.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Every calendar date a pod derives from its own clock can disagree for those 90 seconds around 00:00 UTC: one pod already says tomorrow, so probation flags and document-expiry cutoffs differ by pod, and on the 1st a leave balance jumps by a whole month's accrual on one pod before the other.
keyPoints.quote: Accrual posts at the start of each month.

keyPoints.text: [w2] Each use case turns its injected instant into a UTC date itself unless the caller pins an explicit as-of date, so skew enters exactly where that conversion runs, and a client that needs one answer across pods can pass the date instead of letting the pod pick it.

[w3] Effective-dated terms are protected: creation time only breaks ties between records with the same effective day, and storage refuses a second record for one worker and day, so a skewed creation stamp can never reorder persisted terms.

[w3] Taking 'now' once protects one operation, not two pods: payroll preparation stamps the run and its payslips with one instant and picks the vendor as of that day, so a run is internally consistent, yet which vendor gets pinned for a run prepared at a switch-over midnight depends on which pod served it (stable afterwards, because the run stores its pin).

[w2] Audit ordering is not protected: the org timeline pages newest-first on the entry timestamp with the id as tie-break, and those timestamps come from whichever pod wrote them, so two changes seconds apart on different pods can list in the wrong order; order by a database-assigned sequence, or treat timestamps as approximate within the skew bound.

[w2] Lockout windows: the counters are per process today, a recorded debt whose effect (the threshold multiplied by the node count) dwarfs skew; once they move to a shared store, a lock written with one pod's time and checked with another's runs up to 90 seconds longer or shorter.

[w3] The reproduction is cheap because each use case receives its clock through the constructor: build two instances of the same use case with two frozen clocks 90 seconds apart straddling 00:00 UTC on the 1st, run one query through both, and assert either the divergence you accept or that a pinned as-of date removes it.

questions.prompt: Defend or indict effective dating under a backdated correction: HR backdates a raise by two months. What does the EffectiveFrom fold recompute on its own on every later read, what has already been paid under the old terms and what (if anything) corrects it, and what does a correction workflow need given one-record-per-worker-per-day uniqueness?

keyPoints.text: [w3] Every read with a date on or after the backdated day now resolves to the raise (current terms, any as-of query, the next payroll prepared), because the governing record is chosen from history at read time; the code itself names retroactive raises as the case this shape gets for free.

[w3] The two months already paid do not move: payslips are computed once, when a run is prepared, and can only be attached while the run is a draft, and an executed run is frozen, so nothing in the code computes the difference between old and new terms.

[w3] Even a run not yet executed keeps the stale numbers: preparing a period again returns the existing run, whose identity is cycle plus period start, and a rejection only sends it back to draft with the same payslips, so the runbook's advice to reject and re-prepare with corrected inputs does not recompute anything as the code stands; a correction needs an explicit rebuild of a draft run's payslips.

[w2] Retro pay goes forward: a second run for an already-paid period is refused by that same identity, so the delta lands as a correcting run in a later cycle, documented against the original, and someone (or a new job) must compute terms-as-of-each-paid-period minus what was paid.

[w2] Uniqueness blocks the obvious repair: fixing a mistyped raise on the same effective day is refused as a duplicate, and the code reserves same-day corrections for a deliberate future act, so the workflow needs a supersede operation with its own reason, actor and semantics rather than a second record on a shifted date.

[w2] One time axis has a price: after the backdate, asking for February's terms returns the new salary, and what the system believed when February was paid survives only in the audit trail and the immutable payslips, because the full bitemporal model was consciously declined.
[w1] The backdate is attributable: its audit entry commits with the change or not at all, so the correcting run has a record of who backdated what, and when, to point at.
